assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with endogenous prices and differentiated products (BLP) and dynamic industry models (Ericson-Pakes) changed how competition, mergers and market power are measured. The methods are used in academia, in antitrust and in regulation. Originality, breadth of use and durability are all high.
assessment.attribution: The core BLP contribution is cleanly credited to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also has the dynamic-oligopoly and estimation work. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are important but are more about the wider empirical-IO programme and extensions. A three-name award keeps the credit tied to the method.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from the mid-1990s. The methods have had decades of replication, refinement and use in policy, so the work is fully confirmed.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to include Bresnahan for the 'new empirical IO' programme instead of Levinsohn.
Whether structural IO is seen as methodological craft rather than a discovery.
The pooled candidate covers several distinct strands, so the unit of the prize is not obvious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Technology, trade exposure and task content explain wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment. The work has had very large academic and policy influence. The China-shock literature changed the debate on trade, and the task and skill-premium framework changed the understanding of technological change.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the China shock. Hanson is a co-author on the trade-shock work, and Katz is a pillar of the skill-premium and education-technology literature. Dorn is a key co-author on the China shock, and the final three-name cut is a judgment call. Some task-model credit (Acemoglu, Autor-Levy-Murnane) lies outside the listed names.
assessment.maturity: The papers date from the 1990s to 2013 and have been tested extensively. Parts of the China-shock interpretation are still debated, but the core findings have held up.
uncertainties: Dorn versus Katz for the third slot.
Overlap with the Goldin-related inequality work that has already been recognised.
Ongoing debate over the persistence and external validity of the shock estimates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral-constraint amplification (Kiyotaki-Moore) and the financial accelerator explain credit cycles and how small shocks become large downturns. They became the foundation for post-2008 macro-finance models and for policy work on balance sheets and financial stability. The conceptual originality is high.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a clear and compact claim. Gertler's contribution runs through the financial accelerator work with Bernanke and through later macro-finance models. Bernanke was recognised in 2022, which complicates the credit. Gilchrist is empirically important but secondary.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly three decades old. Its use has been validated through the 2007-09 crisis and the large literature that followed.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize for banks and financial crises, which weakens novelty relative to other candidates.
Whether Gertler is included as a third laureate, given that Bernanke is a co-author of the accelerator papers.
Gertler also appears in the New Keynesian candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance showed systematically how investor protection, legal origin and ownership structure relate to financial development. It created a large cross-country research programme in corporate finance, law and development, and reoriented how institutions are measured. This is a field I know well, so I discount my own enthusiasm.
assessment.attribution: The LLSV papers are collectively authored, so the core trio (La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer) has the strongest claim. Vishny is part of the original quartet, and the 'LLSV' attribution is awkward with a three-name cap. Shleifer has additional influential contributions in behavioural finance and corporate governance.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 1997-2008 and is well established. The legal-origins causal interpretation has been challenged on identification and on whether the effects persist.
uncertainties: Serious replication and identification critiques of the legal-origins thesis.
Whether the committee treats the contribution as a durable empirical regularity or a contested hypothesis.
Reputational concerns about one candidate, which I do not adjudicate here.
Excluding Vishny splits the original four-author team.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Misallocation across firms is a quantitative explanation of cross-country TFP and income differences. It links micro-level distortions to aggregate development outcomes and gave policy-relevant measurement tools. The influence on growth and development economics has been wide.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the most visible paper. Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) developed the same idea independently and at the same time, so shared credit is reasonable. Other contributors outside the list have claims as well.
assessment.maturity: The papers date from 2008-09. A large literature has applied and extended the idea, but the interpretation of measured misallocation is still debated.
uncertainties: Measurement error and the interpretation of dispersion in marginal products are contested.
The work is somewhat recent compared with the oldest candidates.
Whether the committee sees the contribution as a measurement framework or a full theory of development.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade theory explains who exports, how trade reallocates resources across firms, and the productivity gains from trade. It moved trade analysis from the industry level to the firm level, with the rest of the field following. It is clearly original and has had a broad empirical and policy effect.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman has a broad record on firm heterogeneity, including Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI. Redding is influential on quantitative extensions but is less central. Krugman's 2008 prize partly overlaps in subject, which limits novelty.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years old and heavily tested. The structure has been integrated into mainstream quantitative trade.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2008 prize for new trade theory.
Whether Bernard-Jensen-type empirical precursors are given credit outside the list.
Helpman also appears in the political-economy trade candidate, which fragments his profile.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Empirical optimal taxation, the elasticity of taxable income and the sufficient-statistics approach connect tax theory to measurable behavioural responses, and they shaped tax-policy debate. The influence on public economics and on practice is large.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod has the earlier work on tax avoidance and taxable-income responses. Saez has the empirical and theoretical optimal-tax work, and Chetty's sufficient-statistics formulation is distinct. Stantcheva is excluded as relatively early in her career. Saez and Chetty also appear in other candidates, so the credit is spread across several strands.
assessment.maturity: The core work runs from the 1990s to the 2010s. Elasticity estimates and their policy use are still debated, so full confirmation is mixed for the most recent parts.
uncertainties: Identification of taxable-income elasticities is contested.
Credit overlaps with the inequality and mobility candidates.
Whether the committee prefers to honour Mirrlees-style theory instead, which is not on this list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification showed what can be learned from data under credible, weak assumptions. It changed the way applied researchers think about the trade-off between assumption strength and conclusion credibility. Manski's foundational contribution is original and broadly relevant, including for policy analysis under uncertainty.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear pioneer, from the reflection problem, bounds and identification analysis, to treatment-choice decisions. Tamer and Molinari developed the modern econometric theory of moment inequalities and inference. The two-name cut is a judgment on which contribution is distinct; Molinari is a strong alternative.
assessment.maturity: Manski's work dates from the late 1980s onward. The inference literature is more recent and still developing, and applied adoption is real but narrower than that of mainstream methods.
uncertainties: Applied uptake is still limited compared with other econometric methods.
Whether the prize should go to Manski alone as the originator.
Competition from other econometric candidates, such as weak instruments, quantile regression and ML causal inference.
